result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.minimum_branching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a minimum-weight branching of a directed graph (Edmonds' algorithm). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L60842-L60905){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.minimum_branching(weight_attr=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum branching](/assets/graphs/minimum-branching.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A weighted directed triangle: A→B (−2), A→C (−1), C→B (−3), and B→C (4). Only negative edges lower the total, and each node may keep one parent, so the minimum branching takes C→B and A→C, in the accent color, while A→B and B→C are faded. The card lists the two edges and their total weight −3 − 1 = −4." width="100%"} A branching is a directed forest in which every node has at most one incoming edge. The minimum branching has the smallest possible total weight. Because the empty branching (no edges at all) has weight zero, only edges with *negative* weight can lower the total, so on a graph whose weights are all positive the result has no edges. That matches NetworkX, and makes this method useful mainly for signed costs (negative values meaning gains). To connect every node as cheaply as possible, use `minimum_spanning_arborescence()` instead. Self-loops are never chosen, and the original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding the weights. If `None` (the default), each edge's weight field is used (`1.0` on an unweighted graph). Edges that lack the attribute, or hold a non-numeric value, count as `1.0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new directed graph with every node of the original (IDs, labels and attributes kept) and only the branching's edges (weights and attributes copied). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected or an edge value is NaN. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The minimum branching is the maximum branching for the negated weights, found with Edmonds' cycle-contraction algorithm in $O(V E)$ time; see `maximum_branching()`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} With signed costs, the method keeps the profitable (negative) edges, as long as no node gets two parents and no cycle forms: ::: {#2e11f621 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B", -2.0), ("C", "B", -3.0), ("A", "C", -1.0), ("B", "C", 4.0)]) # B takes its cheaper parent C (-3), and C keeps A (-1): total -4 g.minimum_branching().get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['C->B', 'A->C'] ``` ::: ::: When every weight is positive, no edge lowers the total, so the result is empty: ::: {#f089d17d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} positive = ec.Graph(directed=True, weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B"]) positive.add_edge("A", "B", weight=1.0) positive.minimum_branching().count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 0 ``` ::: :::
